#USPol #Michigan

Abdul El-Sayed argues that doctors who attended 'whole a-- medical school' should make treatment decisions without government interference, citing his own medical education as proof of qualified insight.

El-Sayed has never held a medical license in Michigan or New York. His clinical experience consists of a single four-week sub-internship, rendering his claim to clinical practitioner authority deceptive.
Resulting Judgement: (-0.78, -0.82) — Lesser Evil

Verdict: FAIL — The Path of Deception. El-Sayed leverages the perceived authority of a practicing physician while lacking the medical licensure and clinical experience required to claim that status.

- El-Sayed Campaign: FAIL (-0.78, -0.82) — Credentials inflated to shield policy.
- Public Health Framing: FAIL (-0.65, -0.70) — Clinical authority claimed without license.

During a rally at Michigan State University, Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed cited his medical degree from Columbia to argue against state regulation of youth gender procedures, despite lacking a license to practice medicine.

The Bright Side:
El-Sayed holds legitimate advanced degrees in public health and medicine, giving him academic insight into institutional healthcare policy even if he lacks clinical practice experience.

The Breakdown & Plane Error:
This is a Metaphysical Plane error (Q1). The candidate switches academic public health credentials for active clinical authority, using the prestige of medical practice to deflect scrutiny of controversial policies.

Social Physics Analysis:
The candidate executes a Smart Selfish Maneuver. By projecting the persona of a battle-tested physician ('whole a-- doctor'), El-Sayed deflects legitimate regulatory debates into a false binary between medical expertise and political interference, concealing his own lack of clinical license.

The Trajectory: The Path of Deception.
When you map the gap between stated intentions and ground-level results, it plots a direct trajectory toward Lesser Evil. Credential inflation destroys public trust in medical governance.

The Unavoidable Truth: Holding a medical degree does not make one a licensed practicing physician.
The Unavoidable Lie: Claiming medical school attendance grants permanent clinical authority over policy.
